newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian woman on trial for keeping child in box.
newsitem.headline: Austrian woman on trial for keeping child in box.

text.p: An Austrian woman accused of torturing her adopted, mentally handicapped daughter for years and locking her in a coffin-shaped box at night went on trial in Vienna on Wednesday.
The woman named only as Ernestine K, 65, is charged with instigating the abuse of her daughter Maria, now 22, who is 50 to 60 percent mentally disabled.
In a video testimony to the court, Maria, who is undergoing psychiatric treatment, said she had been terrified of "Mummy", a former religious education teacher.
Asked what "Mummy" used to do to her, Maria said: "She beat me, kicked me in the stomach, pulled my ears and tore my hair."
Ernestine's husband Walter is also charged with abuse and incarceration, while family friend Irmengard M. is accused of being an accomplice.
The wooden box, measuring 160 cm by 55 cm and 33 cm deep, (64 inches by 22 and 13.2 deep) with 14 holes for air and a bolt on the outside, stood in a corner of the courtroom.
Maria said her mother would lock her in the box as punishment "for wanting more food or for talking too much".
She would bang on the box lid, crying and shouting but no one came to her rescue, she said.
"I could only hear voices outside, no one could hear me."

Prosecutor Michael Klackl alleged Ernestine began beating Maria in 1984 and frequently locked her in a garden shed with her hands tied together and her mouth sealed with sticking plaster when the couple went out.
"Ernestine robbed Maria of her childhood, youth and self-confidence, and her accomplices went along with it," Klackl said.
Walter and Irmengard admitted in court that they had not dared to free Maria.

After Ernestine had the box built in December 1995, Maria spent her nights locked inside until June 1996 when an anonymous call alerted the authorities to her ordeal and she was taken away from her parents' home in a Vienna suburb.
The wooden box was found smeared with excrement and urine and contained blood-stained newspapers inside.
Ernestine denied all the charges except that of locking Maria in the box, saying she had hoped it would make her undersized daughter grow.
"You won't believe it but she grew 14 cm (5.5 inches)," Ernestine, who had adopted six children before Maria, told the court.
The box was intended as a "health bed" and Maria would always insist on being measured when she came out, she said.
"I never found her looking sad when I came to get her out. Sometimes she would say: 'Just a bit longer, Mummy!'"
Ernestine said she had only meant the best for her daughter. "When I think about it now I wonder why I went to so much trouble," she said.
If convicted, Ernestine and her husband could face up to 10 years in jail.
